result: The local-limit argument controls the fraction of vertices in components above a fixed size; it does not put those vertices in one component. To break that inference, compare one cycle of size n with a disjoint union of cycles of length floor(sqrt(n)), adjusting a negligible remainder. Both local weak limits are the bi-infinite path, which is infinite with probability one. The largest component fractions instead tend to one and zero. Thus the missing step for La-Kabkab is a genuine uniqueness/coalescence or sprinkling argument controlling dependencies among mutually preferred edges; local convergence alone cannot provide it.

Tonelli gives integral x*g2(x)dx=sum_(j>=2)(j-1)P(j)=E[K_degree]-1. Since min(x,y)^2<=x*y, the squared Hilbert-Schmidt norm is at most (E[K_degree]-1)^2. Thus finite mean already makes this symmetric integral operator compact. The kernel is also positive semidefinite because min(x,y)=integral_0^infinity 1_(t<x)*1_(t<y)dt. This removes an exponential moment from the compactness step, while leaving the stronger population conclusions untouched.

Matching this mean to log(n) therefore suggests an apparent positive shift, but it does not derive a connectivity threshold: isolated-vertex probabilities depend on the far lower tail of D, not its mean. Even the candidate central fluctuation law in the separate packet probes deficits of order sqrt(k); isolation requires deficit k, a moving far-tail event outside that limit. An actual sharp-window proof must analyze the relevant order-statistic large deviation and then exclude nontrivial small components.

result: Any connected graph with maximum degree k>=3 has at most 1+k*((k-1)^r-1)/(k-2) vertices within radius r. Hence its diameter d satisfies n<=1+k*((k-1)^d-1)/(k-2), giving a deterministic lower bound of logarithmic order log(n)/log(k). For LK this uses its exact degree cap and requires no independence. A matching upper bound needs expansion of balls grown through mutual rankings; the Erdős-Rényi subgraph used by a coarse coupling may itself be disconnected in the newly covered range and then offers no diameter bound.

Ignoring internal edges among the root preferred neighbors gives D0|X~Bin(k,1-q(X)), where q(X)=E[(X-T)+]/X and T~Beta(k,n-2k). The actual error satisfies E[(D0-D)^2/k]=O(k^2/n+k^5/n^2). Beta central limits and explicit moment controls then give (k-D)/sqrt(k)->g(Z), g(z)=phi(z)+z*Phi(z), with convergence of its first two moments. The variance constant is v=1/3+(sqrt(3)-2)/(2*pi), and the standardized degree limit is (1/sqrt(pi)-g(Z))/sqrt(v), which is non-Gaussian.

independent_check: Upper and lower Chernoff exponents are at least delta^2/(2*k)=3*log(n), followed by a union over n vertices. The deterministic threshold inclusion follows directly from having at most k incident edges below t at each endpoint.

obstruction: A sufficient-condition partial only. Sharp tails and the logarithmic boundary are not determined; below connectivity isolated vertices rule out concentration of every degree near k.
result: Put delta=sqrt(6*k*log(n)) and assume k>2*delta. Threshold edge weights at t=(k-delta)/(n-1). Each threshold degree B_v is binomial with mean k-delta. Chernoff and a union bound give k-2*delta<=B_v<=k for all vertices with probability at least 1-2/n^2. On that event every threshold edge is preferred at both endpoints, so k-2*delta<=D_v<=k simultaneously. Thus k/log(n)->infinity suffices for relative concentration. The argument uses independence of the underlying edge weights, and never independence of vertex degrees.

independent_check: Inclusion-exclusion gives p11=det(Q), p10=Q11-det(Q), p01=Q22-det(Q), p00=det(I-Q); these are a,b,b,a and sum to one. Differentiating H first gives 4*c*log(a/b), independently confirming the second derivative and its sign.

result: The coordinate-diagonal case is a sum of binary entropies, whose second derivatives are -1/[q(1-q)]. There is also an explicit non-diagonal line: for Q(c)=[[1/2,c],[c,1/2]], |c|<1/2, the empty and doubleton probabilities are a=1/4-c^2 and the two singleton probabilities are b=1/4+c^2. Hence H(c)=-2*a*log(a)-2*b*log(b), and Hsecond(c)=4*log(a/b)-8*c^2*(1/a+1/b)<=0. Continuity includes c=+-1/2. This verifies concavity on this affine kernel line. In general the determinant probabilities depend nonlinearly on Q, so concavity of Shannon entropy in a probability vector cannot be applied directly to an arithmetic kernel midpoint.

result: If H2 is spanned by a unit vector u and H1 has finite rank, monotone-couple A with law P_H1 inside C with law P_H. Their deterministic sizes differ by one, so C minus A is a singleton B. At any coordinate e, P(B={e})=P(e in C)-P(e in A)=(P_H)ee-(P_H1)ee=|u(e)|^2. Thus B has precisely P_H2 and (A,B) gives the required coupling in this special case. For higher rank, the same subtraction determines only one-point intensities of C minus A; its higher inclusion probabilities are not fixed. The finite problem can be written as nonnegative weights w(A,B) on disjoint pairs with the three required marginals, but setting up this transportation problem does not prove it feasible.

result: Let f(theta)=g(k*theta). Its Fourier coefficients vanish at lags not divisible by k, so the determinantal kernel is block diagonal on the k residue classes. Determinant factorization proves that these restrictions are independent copies of P_g. If P_g can be represented as F(U_j,...,U_(j+r)) with iid U, define Y_i=F(U_i,U_(i+k),...,U_(i+r*k)). This is a shift-equivariant function of the window U_i,...,U_(i+r*k), so is an (r*k+1)-block factor. The residue-class families use disjoint iid coordinates and have the correct laws. In particular any single-harmonic symbol a+b*cos(k*theta)+c*sin(k*theta) with range in [0,1] inherits the known degree-one construction and is a (k+1)-block factor.

independent_check: For a scalar Q=qI, s_all=q/(1-q) but the conditional probability is q; this catches the odds/probability confusion in the incoming record. In a finite group, equal inverse diagonal entries average to the full matrix trace divided by |Gamma|, irrespective of whether the group is abelian. No sum over one-dimensional characters is substituted for the nonabelian spectrum.
method: Integrator-authored exact special-case argument and failure analysis after checking the incoming source
obstruction: No geometric-mean domination theorem or sharpness certificate. Numerical coupling feasibility is not exact proof, and the infinite-group extension of this particular calculation is not asserted.
result: Put J=Q(I-Q)^(-1). Given the occupied set B outside e, the conditional odds of presence are s_B=J_ee-J_eB*(J_BB)^(-1)*J_Be. Schur-complement minimization makes s_B decrease as B increases. Its minimum is s_all=1/(J^(-1))ee=1/[(Q^(-1))ee-1]. The conditional probability, however, is s_all/(1+s_all)=1/(Q^(-1))ee. Equivariance makes (Q^(-1))ee=tr(Q^(-1)), with normalized trace, so this probability is the harmonic mean h of all eigenvalues counted with multiplicity. Sequential sampling with common independent uniforms couples the process above iid Bernoulli(h), since every conditional probability given a partial reveal is also at least h. Applying the same argument to the complement gives the upper density 1-HM(I-Q). AM-GM applied to the reciprocals gives HM(Q)<=FK(Q), exposing the exact remaining gap.

independent_check: Direct multiplication gives D=[[1/2,-1/2],[-1/2,-1/2]] and D^2=I/2. The right regular representation of S3 contains its two-dimensional irreducible representation, and equivariant operators can independently specify a matrix in that block. On abelian groups the equivariant convolution algebra is commutative, so that setting cannot test this obstruction.
method: Integrator-authored exact special-case argument and failure analysis after checking the incoming source

result: Write D=Q-Qprime. A tempting common upper kernel is R=Qprime+Dplus=(Q+Qprime+|D|)/2. It dominates both in operator order, but need not be a contraction. In dimension two take Q=diag(1,0) and Qprime=(1/2)*[[1,1],[1,1]]. Then D^2=I/2 and |D|=I/sqrt(2). The largest eigenvalue of Q+Qprime is 1+1/sqrt(2), giving lambda_max(R)=1/2+1/sqrt(2)>1. Thus R is not an admissible determinantal kernel and one cannot apply monotone-coupling bounds through it. This same obstruction can be placed in the two-dimensional irreducible block of the right group algebra of S3, with zeros on the other blocks; the resulting operators commute with left translations but not with one another.

result: Partitioning a domain gives independent fine measures multiplied by an independent, spatially varying Gaussian binding field. On each compact subdomain, the weighted mass lies between exp(alpha*inf(Phi)) times its fine total mass and exp(alpha*sup(Phi)) times that mass. These inequalities explain a possible smoothing-transform route, but the weights are functions of position rather than single scalar multipliers of identically distributed masses. Replacing each field by one value creates an oscillation error that must be controlled on the critical tail scale. Multiplying the entire family by a deterministic c>0 preserves the four premises, so the best possible conclusion must allow its tail constant to change by c.

obstruction: The exact Cox-process representation is credited to the source. It is not an explicit solution for rho_D or a closed PDE.
result: Conditional on Z, the extremal leaders form a Poisson process with intensity Z(dx)*exp(-alpha*h)dh. Thus the probability that all heights are at most t is exp(-Z(D)*exp(-alpha*t)/alpha), and the joint maximum density measure is exp(-alpha*t)*E[Z(dx)*exp(-Z(D)*exp(-alpha*t)/alpha)]dt, matching equation12.86. Integrating over t gives the position marginal E[Z(dx)/Z(D)]. This is well-defined although E[Z(D)] is infinite under the source critical-tail law. Consequently a ratio of expectations is unavailable. More generally, a random total mass alone does not forbid equality of such ratios: Z=W*nu for a fixed probability measure nu and integrable positive W is a counterexample to that proposed obstruction.

result: In the limiting decorated Poisson process, restrict leader heights to [-t,H] and let F_s be the number of sites in one cluster within depth s. Conditional on Z, Campbell's formula gives expected truncated count Z(A)*exp(alpha*t)*integral_0^(t+H) exp(-alpha*s)*E[F_s] ds. If E[F_s] is asymptotic to c*exp(alpha*s), this is asymptotic to c*Z(A)*t*exp(alpha*t) when H=o(t), explaining the conjectured t factor. The conditional variance, when finite, is Z(A)*exp(alpha*t)*integral_0^(t+H) exp(-alpha*s)*E[F_s^2] ds. Its negligibility after division by t^2*exp(2*alpha*t), and control of high leaders and finite-N approximation, are additional requirements, not consequences of the first-moment formula.

Its density is the finite sum f_i(omega)=sum_x P_(-x),omega[X_i=0], obtained by changing variables under a spatial shift in the annealed endpoint formula. Set g_n=(1/n)*sum_(i=0)^(n-1) f_i. If these densities are uniformly integrable in L1(P), Dunford-Pettis gives a weak-L1 convergent subsequence g_n to g, with g>=0 and integral g=1. For bounded measurable h, integral(Rh-h)*g_n dP=((P*R^n)h-P h)/n tends to zero. Weak-L1 convergence passes both bounded test functions, so g dP is invariant. A uniform Lp bound for some p>1 would suffice, since integral_(g_n>K) g_n<=K^(1-p)*integral g_n^p. This isolates an explicit missing estimate: positive speed must supply enough control of these occupation densities, not merely weak compactness of the environment space.

result: Uniform ellipticity gives a precise finite-trap bound. Suppose every site of a finite set A has a nearest-neighbor path of at most m steps leading outside A, and every transition probability is at least kappa. At each block of m steps before exit, the conditional probability of leaving is at least kappa^m. The strong Markov property yields P_x,omega[tau_A>j*m]<=(1-kappa^m)^j and E_x,omega[tau_A]<=m*kappa^(-m). For A=[-R,R]^d intersect Z^d, m=2R+1 works by moving along one coordinate. Thus no fixed-size trap has an arbitrarily large quenched mean under uniform ellipticity. But the bound grows exponentially with R; it cannot be summed over the random spatial extent explored before regeneration without a further tail estimate. For coordinate directions, the source renewal formula gives positive speed exactly when the conditional mean regeneration time is finite; almost-sure finite regeneration times alone do not supply it.

If the mean is zero, nearest-neighbor steps force p(e_i)=p(-e_i)>0 for every i. The characteristic function is phi(t)=2*sum_i p(e_i)*cos(t_i). Its absolute value equals1 only at the two torus points with all coordinates0 or all coordinates pi. Taylor expansion at each gives |phi(t)|<=1-c*dist(t,S)^2 locally, while compactness bounds it strictly below1 elsewhere. Fourier inversion therefore bounds the return probability by C*n^(-d/2). The sum over n is finite for d>=3, proving transience through the expected visit count. For a spatially varying environment the quenched increments are no longer iid and there is no one fixed characteristic function whose nth power gives the transition law.

Under initial law Q the variables q(eta_n) all have the same distribution, so q(eta_0) itself must take values only0 and1. The harmonic identity q(omega)=sum_e omega(0,e)*q(t_e omega), together with ellipticity, then forces every neighboring shift to have the same value on a common full-measure set. Spatial ergodicity of P makes q constant, establishing the directional zero-one law in this restricted class. The absent invariant law is the obstruction to applying this stationary argument to all iid environments.
